# STEPFOC

> Documentation for the STEPFOC stepper motor FOC driver by Source Robotics.

Every page of this site is also available as Markdown at its address followed by `index.md`, with its links absolute; `llms-full.txt` holds every page in one file. The version box on the landing page names the release the pages describe.

Full text of every page, in the order of the site's navigation. Source: https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/

reading, and the document history on the About page says what changed. Take care that the firmware version named

between firmware releases. The text and the images are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples MIT.

# Quick start

From the box to a calibrated motor that follows commands, on one page. The quickest way through is
[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) in the browser; every step also shows the terminal commands, and ends with a
link to the chapter that explains it. Follow the link when a step is not clear or something fails.

!!! danger "Read first"
    Reversed supply polarity, a daisy-chain cable the wrong way round, or 5 V on the UART port destroys the driver.
    The motor turns during calibration. The [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/02-safety/) chapter is two minutes long.

## 1. What you need

| | Where to get it |
|---|---|
| **STEPFOC driver** | [single driver](https://source-robotics.com/products/STEPFOC-stepper-controller) or the [starter kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/STEPFOC-starter-kit), which has everything below except the motor and the supply |
| **A bipolar stepper motor** with a rear shaft: NEMA 17, 1 to 5 Ω per coil, 3 A or less | the [tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/tested-motors/) are safe choices |
| **The encoder magnet**, diametrically magnetised; the stock one is 6 × 2.5 mm, another thickness is fine if it gives the 1 mm gap | [magnet](https://source-robotics.com/products/6x2-5mm-diametrical-neodymium-magnet) |
| **A spacer** for your motor length and four longer M3 screws | printable spacers in [Stepper motor accessories](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files/Stepper%20motor%20accessories) |
| **USB-to-serial adapter**, 3.3 V, and its cable | [serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter), [UART cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/uart-cable) |
| **Power cable** | [power cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable) |
| **A 12 to 29 V supply**, 24 V recommended | a bench supply with a current limit is the safest start |
| For CAN later: **CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter** and a **CAN cable** | [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter), [CAN cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable) |
| Optional: **100 kΩ NTC thermistor** for motor temperature protection | [thermistor](https://source-robotics.com/products/100k-ntc-thermistor) |
| **Software**: Motor GUI in Chrome or Edge, or a serial terminal | [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/); PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor or the Arduino serial monitor |

Read in more detail: [What you need](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/01-overview/what-you-need/).

## 2. Fit the magnet

Press the magnet onto the rear shaft, centred, and glue it. It must end up about **1 mm** above the encoder chip
in the middle of the board, and it must not be able to turn on the shaft. A magnet that slips is the usual cause of
a calibration that "succeeds" and a motor that then runs badly.

Read in more detail: [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/magnet/).

## 3. Mount the board

Remove the motor's four rear screws, put the spacer on, the board on the spacer with the encoder chip towards the
magnet, and the longer screws in. Check the gap: 1 mm, not touching.

Read in more detail: [Mounting on the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/mounting/).

## 4. Wire the motor

Find the two coils with a multimeter (the two wires of a coil show a few ohms; wires of different coils show
nothing). Solder one coil to **A+ and A−**, the other to **B+ and B−**. Which coil is which, and which way round,
does not matter: calibration detects it.

Read in more detail: [Wiring the stepper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/wiring/).

## 5. Connect power and the PC

1. The supply to a power connector: **DC+ to positive, DC− to negative**. Check twice.
2. The serial adapter to the UART connector with the UART cable (TX to RX, RX to TX; 3.3 V only).
3. Power on. The LED turns on steadily: the driver is not calibrated yet, which it reports as an error state.
   (The serial adapter alone powers the driver's logic: it answers over UART without the supply, but reports a
   Vbus error and will not calibrate or move.)

=== "Motor GUI"
    Open [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/) in Chrome or Edge, choose the serial connection and **Connect** on
    the adapter's port. The driver's identity and state appear: hardware and firmware version, serial number,
    *Not calibrated*, *No errors*. If nothing connects: the port, the cable's TX/RX, the browser (Web Serial needs
    a Chromium browser).

    Read in more detail: [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/motor-gui/).

=== "Terminal"
    Open a terminal on the adapter's port, 256000 baud, line ending CR+LF, and type `#Info`. The driver prints its
    hardware and firmware version and the state of everything.

    Read in more detail: [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/terminal/).

Read in more detail: [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/power-and-can/) ·
[Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/connectors/).

**Check:** the driver's identity and live state appear before you change settings. A missing connection
is covered in [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/motor-gui/#opening-the-port) or [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/08-troubleshooting/).

## 6. Restore the defaults and enter the motor parameters

First the factory defaults, so that calibration does not start from another motor's values or from junk in the
EEPROM: *Default* in the Motor GUI settings, or `#Default` in the terminal. (It also resets the serial number the
driver reports.) Then the parameters:

From the motor's datasheet, for **one coil**: the pole pairs (50 for a 1.8° motor, 100 for 0.9°), the phase
resistance in ohms, the phase inductance in henries (2.6 mH = 0.0026). STEPFOC does not measure these; calibration
fails on a value left at 0.

=== "Motor GUI"
    Enter *Pole pairs*, *Resistance* and *Inductance* in the motor settings and apply them.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #PP 50
    #R 1.1
    #L 0.0026
    ```

Read in more detail: [Motor parameters and calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/calibration/).

## 7. Calibrate

Fix the motor to the bench, nothing on the shaft, 24 V on the supply.

=== "Motor GUI"
    Start the calibration. The GUI switches to *Calibration mode* and shows the driver's log step by step.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Cal
    ```

The LED flashes, the motor turns in both directions, and the driver reports each step: the pole pairs, the magnet,
the supply, the parameters you entered, the open-loop spin, the angle offset, the motor constants, and finally

```
Calibration success!
Save config with #Save
Going to idle!
```

A failed step names itself. `Magnet test: Failed` is the magnet; `Open loop: Failed` or `Phase order is wrong!`
means the motor did not turn or did not respond: check the four wires, the supply, and that the magnet does not
slip.

Read in more detail: [Motor parameters and calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/calibration/), with the whole log and every
message.

**Check:** the calibration log ends with `Calibration success!`. If it does not, use the failed step in
[Calibration troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/calibration/#troubleshooting); do not treat a stopped motor as success.

## 8. Set the current limit and save

The current limit is the motor's rated phase current in mA; the firmware's default is higher than a small motor's
rating.

=== "Motor GUI"
    Set the current limit in the limits, then **Save** (the GUI warns about unsaved changes until you do).

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #Ilim 1500
    #Save
    ```

Without saving, the calibration is gone at the next power cycle. The LED now shows three short flashes and a
pause: normal operation.

Read in more detail: [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/tuning/) ·
[Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/saving/).

**Check:** after **Save**, Motor GUI no longer marks unsaved changes. [Saving](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/saving/) explains
which settings are kept.

## 9. Move it

=== "Motor GUI"
    Use the jog controls: *Jog velocity* turns the motor at a speed, *Jog position* moves it to a position, *Jog
    current* applies a torque; *Send setpoint* sends a value in the current control mode. The plots show position,
    speed and current while it moves.

=== "Terminal"
    ```
    #V 16384        one revolution per second
    #V 0
    #P 0            back to where it started
    #P 16384        one revolution forward
    #Idle
    ```

Position is in encoder ticks, 16384 per revolution; speed in ticks per second; current in mA. If the motor hums
or whines, lower the current limit or tune the loops.

Read in more detail: [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/modes/) · [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/tuning/).

**Check:** the position/speed feedback follows the request, and **Idle** stops driving the motor. A motor
that does not follow needs [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/08-troubleshooting/) before a load is attached.

## 10. Where to go next

| You want to | Read |
|---|---|
| get to know Motor GUI: the screen, the plots, recordings, several motors | [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/motor-gui/), [Working in Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/motor-gui/) |
| control the driver from a program over CAN | [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/can/), then [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/python/) |
| put several drivers on one bus | give each a node ID and terminate the ends: [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/power-and-can/) |
| protect the motor from overheating | [Thermistor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/thermistor/) |
| update the firmware | [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/07-firmware/) |
| look up a message or a command | [API reference](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/reference/) |
| understand why it does not work | [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/errors/), [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/08-troubleshooting/) |

# About this manual

## Scope and audience

The STEPFOC Manual covers the STEPFOC stepper driver from unpacking to a tuned motor on a CAN bus: what the driver
is, how to mount it on a motor and wire it, the first setup over the serial terminal, calibration and tuning, how
the driver is controlled over UART and CAN or from Python, and how its firmware is updated. The Reference lists
every CAN message and UART command of the firmware release named on the landing page. The Guides are worked
examples.

It is written for someone who builds a robot or a machine with STEPFOC: a maker, a student or an engineer who can
solder four motor wires and open a serial terminal. It does not assume any knowledge of field-oriented control; the
Theory corner in the appendix explains the concepts the control modes rely on.

Read the Safety chapter before you power anything. The [Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/quick-start/) is the whole first setup on one page; the chapters are in the order you need them and go deeper.

## Finding your way

The header has four tabs. **STEPFOC Manual** is the document you read from the start: the quick start, then
safety, technical data, mounting, the first setup, operation and firmware updates, in numbered chapters. Motor
GUI, the tool in the browser, is the usual way to do what the chapters describe; each procedure shows it first
and the terminal command beside it. **API reference** lists every CAN message, every UART command and the Python
library's calls for the firmware release this site describes, with the defaults and the error flags, and is where
you look things up. **Guides** are worked examples with code. **Support** says where to get help and how to report
a problem.

The whole site describes one firmware release. The dropdown next to the site name switches between releases, and a
page from an older release says so in a bar at the top. The repository card on the right of the header opens the
firmware repository; every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report a problem with it.
## Warnings and notes

Three kinds of highlighted text appear in this documentation. Read every Danger and Notice before you act on the
step it belongs to.

!!! note "Note"
    Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

!!! warning "Notice"
    The robot, the tool, or data on the control box can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

!!! danger "Danger"
    Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.
## Related documents

| Document | Number | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| STEPFOC Manual | SR-5001 | the STEPFOC stepper driver: quick start, safety, technical data, mounting, setup with Motor GUI or a terminal, operation, firmware; the API reference; guides |

A document marked with a firmware version describes that firmware release, here 108; the version selector in the header switches between releases. The compatibility table says which firmware, Python library and hardware revisions work together.

The Spectral Micro BLDC driver has similar hardware and firmware and is run the same way; its documentation is at
[docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/). The grippers
driven by STEPFOC electronics are documented at
[docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/).

## Document history

The STEPFOC Manual describes one firmware release; one revision is kept per release, and the version selector in
the header switches between them. The earlier version of this site, for firmware 103, is kept as version `103`.

The text and the images of this documentation are licensed under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), the code examples under the [MIT licence](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-docs/blob/main/LICENSE-CODE). The Source Robotics name, the product names and the logos are not covered by either.

# Overview

What STEPFOC is and what it is made of, how it relates to the Spectral Micro BLDC driver it is built on, and what
you need around it to get a motor turning.

## In this chapter

- [The driver at a glance](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/01-overview/driver-at-a-glance/)
- [STEPFOC and Spectral Micro](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/01-overview/stepfoc-and-spectral/)
- [What you need](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/01-overview/what-you-need/)


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/01-overview/driver-at-a-glance/ -->

# The driver at a glance

STEPFOC is a field-oriented controller for bipolar stepper motors. It sits on the back of a NEMA 17 motor, reads
the rotor position from a magnet on the motor shaft, and drives the two coils with sinusoidal currents the way a
servo drive does, instead of the fixed step currents of a conventional stepper driver. The result is a stepper that
runs quietly and efficiently, never loses steps, reports its position, and can be commanded in position, speed,
current (torque) or impedance.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The STEPFOC driver](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/STEPFOC.webp){ width="520" }
  <figcaption>Figure 1: The STEPFOC driver, 39 × 39 mm, with the encoder chip in the middle of the board.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What is on the board

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| STM32F103CB microcontroller | runs the control loops at 6250 Hz and the CAN and UART interfaces |
| 14-bit magnetic encoder (MT6816) | reads the position of the magnet on the motor shaft: 16384 ticks per revolution |
| H-bridge driver with inline current sensing | drives the two coils with up to 2.8 A and measures the phase currents |
| 16 Kbit EEPROM | keeps the configuration and the calibration over a power cycle |
| Two CAN connectors and two power connectors | daisy-chain several drivers on one bus and one supply |
| CAN termination switch | the 120 Ω resistor the first and the last node need |
| UART connector (3.3 V) | the serial terminal: every setting, calibration, tuning |
| Thermistor connector | an NTC on the motor for temperature protection |
| ADDITIONAL2 pin | an input or output you can use: HALL mode homes against a sensor wired here |
| JTAG connector (1.27 mm) | the programming adapter, for installing the bootloader or for development |
| Status LED | normal operation, calibration or error, see below |

The connectors and their pinout are in [Connectors and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/connectors/).

## What the firmware does

The firmware closes three nested loops on the motor: a current (torque) loop, a velocity loop around it and a
position loop around that, plus an impedance (PD) loop that makes the motor behave like a spring and damper.
A command picks the loop: a current setpoint, a speed, a position or a PD setpoint. Open-loop stepping, a
voltage-torque mode and a homing mode against a sensor exist beside them; [Control modes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/modes/)
describes each.

The driver protects itself and the motor: it stops on a supply voltage outside the limits, on an encoder fault, on
an over-speed, on a motor over-temperature (with the thermistor), on a hardware fault of the driver stage, on an
E-stop command and on a watchdog that runs out. The status LED and `#Error` tell which; see
[Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/errors/).

## How it is controlled

- **UART**, a 3.3 V serial port at 256000 baud: human-readable commands such as `#P 16384`, and the only way to
  run the calibration. See [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/uart/).
- **CAN**, 1 Mbit/s, up to 16 drivers on one bus: compact frames for real-time control from a PC with the CANvas
  adapter, a microcontroller or a robot control box. See [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/can/).
- **Python**, the `Spectral-BLDC` library on top of CAN. See [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/python/).
- **Motor GUI**, in the browser, over serial or CAN: the usual tool for setup, testing and tuning. See [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/motor-gui/).

## The status LED

| Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|
| three short flashes and a pause | normal operation: no error, calibrated |
| flashing every 0.5 s | the calibration routine is running |
| on, not flashing | error mode: at least one error is active, or the motor is not calibrated |

The LED can be turned off with `#LED 0`.

| Normal operation | Calibration | Error mode |
|---|---|---|
| ![Three short flashes and a pause](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/Normal.webp){ width="180" } | ![Flashing every 0.5 s](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/Calib.webp){ width="180" } | ![On, steady](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/Error2.webp){ width="180" } |


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/01-overview/stepfoc-and-spectral/ -->

# STEPFOC and Spectral Micro

STEPFOC and the [Spectral Micro BLDC driver](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/) are sister
drivers: similar hardware and similar firmware, each made for its kind of motor. The Spectral Micro drives
three-phase brushless motors; STEPFOC drives two-phase stepper motors. They are not the same board and do not run
the same firmware, but they are controlled and run practically the same way: the same CAN and UART commands, the
same Python library, Motor GUI and bootloader.

What this means in practice:

- **The commands are practically the same.** The CAN messages and UART commands of the Reference have the same
  IDs, names and layouts on both drivers; STEPFOC adds a few that only make sense on a stepper (homing against a
  sensor, open-loop stepping). A program written for one runs on the other.
- **The firmware releases go in step.** A STEPFOC release has a Spectral Micro counterpart with the same changes;
  the [compatibility table](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/appendix/compatibility/) lists the pairs. The numbers differ by one (STEPFOC 108
  is Spectral Micro 107).
- **Calibration differs.** A BLDC driver measures the motor's resistance and inductance and finds its pole pairs;
  STEPFOC cannot, so you enter the three values from the motor's datasheet before calibrating. See
  [Motor parameters and calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/calibration/).
- **The motor terminals differ.** A+, A−, B+, B− for the two stepper coils instead of U, V, W.
- **Some images on this site show a Spectral Micro.** Where a photo or a screenshot shows the BLDC board, the
  procedure is the same for STEPFOC.

The guides under the Guides tab were written with the Spectral Micro; the code in them runs unchanged on STEPFOC.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/01-overview/what-you-need/ -->

# What you need

This page lists what a STEPFOC setup is made of, what comes with the driver, and what you buy or make yourself.

## The driver

STEPFOC is sold as a single driver or as a starter kit in the Source Robotics shop:

- [STEPFOC stepper driver](https://source-robotics.com/products/STEPFOC-stepper-controller)
- [STEPFOC starter kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/STEPFOC-starter-kit), which adds the adapters, the
  magnet, the cables and a thermistor listed below

Every driver is end-of-line tested and ships with the current firmware release and the bootloader already
installed, so a driver works out of the box with a serial terminal, the Python library or Motor GUI. The firmware
can be updated later without a programming adapter; see [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/07-firmware/).

## A stepper motor

STEPFOC drives bipolar (4-wire) stepper motors. It is made for the NEMA 17 frame, whose mounting holes match the
board, and it also works with NEMA 14 and NEMA 23 motors on an adapter. Look for a motor with a phase resistance
of 1 to 5 Ω and a rated current of 3 A or less; the [tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/tested-motors/) are
known to work.

## The encoder magnet

A diametrically magnetised 6 × 2.5 mm neodymium magnet on the rear of the motor shaft, about 1 mm above the
encoder chip in the middle of the board: [6 × 2.5 mm diametrical magnet](https://source-robotics.com/products/6x2-5mm-diametrical-neodymium-magnet).
An axially magnetised magnet, or one that wobbles, makes calibration fail or report bad positions. The 6 × 2.5 mm size is
the stock one, not a requirement: another thickness is a way to set the 1 mm gap when a shaft or a spacer leaves the
wrong distance.
[The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/magnet/) says how to fit it.

## Adapters and cables

| Part | Needed for | Shop |
|---|---|---|
| USB-to-serial adapter (3.3 V) | the serial terminal: calibration, tuning, any `#` command | [Serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter) |
| CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter | CAN control from a PC, the Python library, Motor GUI over CAN | [CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) |
| CAN cable and power cable | daisy-chaining several drivers | [CAN cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable), [power cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable) |
| 100 kΩ NTC thermistor | motor temperature protection (optional but recommended) | [Thermistor](https://source-robotics.com/products/100k-ntc-thermistor) |
| JTAG programming adapter | only for installing the bootloader on an older board, or for firmware development | [Programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/jtag-programming-adapter-1-27-pitch) |

!!! danger "Cable orientation"
    The daisy-chain cables for CAN and power are keyed by their orientation, not by their connector. A cable
    plugged in the wrong way round destroys the driver. Use the cables from the shop or follow
    [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/power-and-can/) exactly when you make your own.

## A power supply

12 to 29 V DC, 24 V recommended; see [Ratings and limits](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/ratings/). Calibrate at 24 V:
the motor constants come out wrong at a lower voltage. A bench supply with a current limit is the safest way to
start.

## Software

- [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), in the browser, over the serial adapter or the CAN adapter: the usual tool
  for setup, calibration, tuning, plots and firmware updates; see [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/motor-gui/).
- Or a serial terminal: PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor in VS Code, or the Arduino serial monitor; see
  [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/terminal/).
- The Python library `Spectral-BLDC` for CAN control from your own programs; see [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/python/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/02-safety/ -->

# Safety

STEPFOC is a bare circuit board that drives a motor from a supply of up to 29 V. Read this chapter before you
connect anything; the few rules here are the ones that destroy a driver, a motor or a finger when they are ignored.

## Electrical

!!! danger "Supply polarity"
    Reversing the polarity on DC+ and DC− destroys the driver at once. Check the polarity of every power cable
    before you plug it in, every time.

!!! danger "Cable orientation on the daisy chain"
    The CAN and power cables that link one driver to the next are keyed by their orientation, not by their
    connector: a cable plugged in the wrong way round puts the supply on the wrong pins and destroys the driver.
    Use the cables from the Source Robotics shop, or make yours exactly as shown in
    [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/power-and-can/).

!!! danger "UART is 3.3 V"
    The UART port runs at 3.3 V. A 5 V serial adapter destroys the board. Use a 3.3 V adapter, such as the one
    from the shop.

!!! warning "Supply voltage"
    12 to 29 V DC. The driver raises a Vbus error outside 9 to 29.5 V, but the hardware limit is 29 V: do not
    connect a supply that can rise above it, and allow for the voltage a decelerating motor pushes back into the
    supply. A bench supply with a current limit is the safest way to start.

!!! warning "Do not disconnect a running motor"
    Never unplug a motor, or a power cable in the daisy chain, while the driver is powered. The inductive kick of
    the coils and the arcing at the connector damage the driver stage.

## Mechanical

!!! danger "Moving parts"
    A calibrating or running motor turns without warning, in both directions, and the stepper in position mode
    pushes back hard against a hand. Keep fingers, hair and cables away from the shaft and whatever is mounted on
    it, fix the motor to the bench before the first test, and test without a load on the shaft.

!!! warning "The encoder magnet"
    The magnet sits about 1 mm above the encoder chip. A magnet that touches the chip, or sits far too close, can
    damage the microcontroller; a magnet too far away gives a wrong position. Mount it as described in
    [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/magnet/).

!!! warning "Hot motor and driver"
    A stepper running at its rated current gets hot enough to burn. Set the current limit for your motor
    ([Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/tuning/)), use the thermistor, and give the driver airflow when it
    runs near 2.8 A.

## Stopping the motor

- `Send_ESTOP` over CAN, or `#Idle` over UART, stops the motor at once; the E-stop error stays until it is cleared.
- Cutting the supply stops the motor as well; a stepper then holds nothing, so a vertical axis drops.
- The watchdog ([Send_Watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/reference/can/system/)) stops the motor by itself when the host stops talking.

Nothing on the driver is a certified safety function. A machine that can hurt someone needs an emergency stop
that cuts the motor supply, independent of the driver.

## Firmware updates and programming

When you connect a programming adapter to the JTAG connector, disconnect the motor supply and the UART adapter
first. Updating over the bootloader needs no adapter; see [Firmware](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/07-firmware/).

## Liability

STEPFOC is sold as a component for people who build their own machines. Its hardware designs, firmware and this
documentation are under development and may contain errors.
Whoever builds a machine with it is responsible for its safe design, assembly and operation.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/ -->

# Technical data

The numbers: ratings and limits, the connectors with their pinout, the dimensions, and the motors that have been
tested with the driver.

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/ratings/ -->

# Ratings and limits

## Electrical

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Supply voltage | 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V typical |
| Vbus error limits (firmware) | below 9 V or above 29.5 V |
| Phase current, continuous | 1.5 A typical |
| Phase current, maximum | 2.8 A, the firmware's limit (`#Ilim` is clamped to 2800 mA); needs good cooling and short bursts |
| Power, maximum | 80 W |
| Power, idle | 0.3 W |
| PWM frequency | 25 kHz |
| Control loop frequency | 6250 Hz |
| Electrical frequency, maximum | 600 Hz |
| Current sensing | inline, both phases |
| Encoder | 14-bit magnetic, 16384 ticks per revolution, diametrical magnet 1 mm above the chip |
| UART | 3.3 V, 256000 baud by default (1 000 000 tested) |
| CAN | CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers, node IDs 0 to 15, 120 Ω termination by switch |
| Thermistor input | 100 kΩ NTC, 54.9 kΩ pull-down |
| ADDITIONAL2 | analog input or general-purpose input/output, 3.3 V |
| Driver stage protection | hardware overcurrent, undervoltage and overtemperature shutdown; shown as a driver error |

!!! warning "Reversing the polarity on DC+ and DC− destroys the board."

## Thermal and environmental

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Operating temperature of the board | −20 to 130 °C |
| Motor temperature limit (firmware, with the thermistor) | 75 °C by default (`#Tlim`), −20 °C minimum |

## Mechanical

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Dimensions | 39 × 39 mm |
| Mass | 8 g |
| Mounting | the NEMA 17 pattern, 31 mm hole spacing; NEMA 14 and 23 motors with an adapter |

## Firmware limits

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Position | signed 24-bit over CAN (±8.4 million ticks, ±512 revolutions), 32-bit internally |
| Speed | signed 24-bit over CAN, encoder ticks per second |
| Current setpoint | signed 16-bit over CAN, mA |
| Pole pairs accepted by calibration | 50, 75, 100 or 125 |
| Configuration | kept in the EEPROM with `#Save` / `Send_Save_config` |

The defaults of every setting are listed in the [Defaults](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/reference/defaults/) reference.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/connectors/ -->

# Connectors and pinout

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The connectors of the STEPFOC driver](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/STEPFOC_CONN.webp){ width="900" }
  <figcaption>Figure 2: The connectors. The motor coils go to A+, A−, B+, B−; the supply to DC+ and DC−.</figcaption>
</figure>

| Connector | Pins | Type | Cable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Motor | A+, A−, B+, B− | solder pads | the motor's own leads, see [Wiring the stepper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/wiring/) |
| Power, two of them | DC+, DC− | JST XH, 2 pins | [Power cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable); the second connector feeds the next driver |
| CAN, two of them | CAN H, CAN L | JST ZH, 2 pins | [CAN cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable); the second connector feeds the next driver |
| UART | 3.3 V, TX, RX, GND | JST SH, 4 pins | [UART cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/uart-cable) |
| Thermistor | NTC, NTC | JST SH, 2 pins | the 100 kΩ NTC from the shop or any 100 kΩ NTC |
| JTAG | 3.3 V, GND, SWDIO, SWCLK | 1.27 mm header | [Programming adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/jtag-programming-adapter-1-27-pitch) |
| ADDITIONAL2 | signal, GND | pads | your sensor; the HALL homing mode reads this pin |
| STEP / DIR | STEP, DIR, GND, 24 V | header | hardware only: the firmware does not support a step/dir interface |

!!! danger "Polarity and orientation"
    DC+ to the positive supply, DC− to the negative; a cable the wrong way round destroys the driver. The daisy-chain
    cables have an orientation too: see [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/power-and-can/).

!!! note
    - UART is TX to RX and RX to TX between the driver and the adapter.
    - The UART port and the ADDITIONAL2 pin are 3.3 V. 5 V on either destroys the board.
    - The thermistor pin has a 54.9 kΩ pull-down; the firmware's temperature table is for a 100 kΩ NTC.
    - The CAN termination switch is next to the CAN connectors; **ON** connects the 120 Ω resistor.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/dimensions/ -->

# Dimensions and CAD

The board is 39 × 39 mm with the four mounting holes on the NEMA 17 pattern (31 mm apart), so it bolts to the back
of a NEMA 17 motor with the motor's own screws and a spacer. The encoder chip is exactly in the middle of the board,
on the motor shaft's axis.

  </div>

</div>

  ![Dimensions of the board](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/micro_dimensions.webp){ width="600" }
  <figcaption>Figure 3: Board dimensions and hole pattern. The drawing is of the Spectral Micro, which has the same outline and hole pattern.</figcaption>
</figure>

The STEP files of the board, the magnet spacers for different motor lengths and the tool for pressing the magnet
onto the shaft are in the firmware repository:

- [Stepper motor accessories](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files/Stepper%20motor%20accessories):
  magnet spacers, NEMA 17 spacers for different motor lengths, NEMA 23 spacers
- [Tools](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files/Tools): the magnet tool

[CAD and downloads](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/cad-files/) lists everything that can be downloaded.

# Tested motors

STEPFOC works with bipolar (4-wire) stepper motors whose phase resistance is 1 to 5 Ω and whose rated current is
3 A or less. The motors below have been run on it; the resistance and inductance are the datasheet values of one
coil, which is what you enter with `#R` and `#L` before calibration.

| | Motor | Frame | Pole pairs | Phase resistance | Phase inductance | Rated current | Mass | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ![17HS08-1004S](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/17HS08-1004S.webp){ width="90" } | 17HS08-1004S | NEMA 17, 20 mm | 50 | 3.7 Ω | 4.5 mH | 1.0 A | 140 g | [Stepperonline](https://www.omc-stepperonline.com/nema-17-bipolar-1-8deg-16ncm-22-6oz-in-1a-3-7v-42x42x20mm-4-wires-17hs08-1004s) |
| ![17HS16-2004S1](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/17HS16-2004S1.webp){ width="90" } | 17HS16-2004S1 | NEMA 17, 40 mm | 50 | 1.1 Ω | 2.6 mH | 2.0 A | 310 g | [Stepperonline](https://www.omc-stepperonline.com/nema-17-bipolar-45ncm-64oz-in-2a-42x42x40mm-4-wires-w-1m-cable-connector-17hs16-2004s1) |
| ![17HS24-2104S](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/17HS24-2104S.webp){ width="90" } | 17HS24-2104S | NEMA 17, 60 mm | 50 | 1.6 Ω | 3.0 mH | 2.1 A | 500 g | [Stepperonline](https://www.omc-stepperonline.com/nema-17-bipolar-1-8deg-65ncm-92oz-in-2-1a-3-36v-42x42x60mm-4-wires-17hs24-2104s) |
| ![23HM22-2804S](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/23HM22-2804S.webp){ width="90" } | 23HM22-2804S | NEMA 23, 56 mm, 0.9° | 100 | 1.16 Ω | 4.2 mH | 2.8 A | 700 g | [Stepperonline](https://www.omc-stepperonline.com/nema-23-bipolar-0-9deg-1-26nm-178-4oz-in-2-8a-2-5v-57x57x56mm-4-wires-23hm22-2804s) |

Before the first test, set the current limit to the motor's rated current with `#Ilim`; the firmware's default is
higher than the 17HS08's rating. See [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/tuning/).

!!! tip "Choosing a motor"
    A lower phase resistance and inductance give a higher speed at a given supply voltage; the velocity constant
    `KV` that calibration finds tells how fast the motor can turn: roughly 0.8 × Vbus × KV revolutions per minute.
    Motors with visibly uneven windings or a resistance that differs between the two coils calibrate badly.

# Mounting and wiring

How the driver goes onto the motor and what gets connected to it: the encoder magnet on the shaft, the board on
the motor's back, the two coils to the motor terminals, the supply and the CAN bus, and the thermistor. Do the
pages in order; the magnet first, because it is the one thing you cannot check from the outside later.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Hardware setup video](https://img.youtube.com/vi/60UMc95H8iE/hqdefault.jpg){ width="480" }
  <figcaption>Figure 5: <a href="https://youtu.be/60UMc95H8iE">The motor hardware setup video</a> shows the whole procedure on a NEMA 17 motor.</figcaption>
</figure>

## In this chapter

- [The encoder magnet](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/magnet/)
- [Mounting on the motor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/mounting/)
- [Wiring the stepper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/wiring/)
- [Power and the CAN daisy chain](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/power-and-can/)
- [Thermistor](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/thermistor/)

When all of it is done, continue with [First setup](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/magnet/ -->

# The encoder magnet

The encoder reads a diametrically magnetised magnet on the rear end of the motor shaft. The magnet must sit
centred on the shaft's axis, parallel to the board, about **1 mm** above the encoder chip, and it must not move.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Magnet distance to the encoder](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/STEPFOC_MAGNET.png){ width="700" }
  <figcaption>Figure 6: About 1 mm between the magnet and the encoder chip in the middle of the board.</figcaption>
</figure>

## The magnet

A neodymium disc, **diametrically** magnetised (north and south across the diameter, not through the thickness).
The shop's [6 × 2.5 mm diametrical magnet](https://source-robotics.com/products/6x2-5mm-diametrical-neodymium-magnet)
is the size the printed spacers are made for. An axially magnetised magnet looks the same and does not work: the
magnet test may even pass, and the position is wrong.

!!! note "The size is not fixed"
    6 × 2.5 mm is the stock size, not a requirement. Any diametrically magnetised disc of about 6 mm diameter
    works, and the thickness is a way to set the gap: a thicker magnet brings its face closer to the encoder, a
    thinner one farther, so with a shaft or a spacer that leaves the wrong distance you can pick the thickness
    that gives 1 mm instead of changing the spacer. What matters is the 1 mm from the magnet's face to the chip,
    the magnet centred on the shaft, and the diametrical magnetisation.

## Fitting it

1. The motor needs a rear shaft. Most NEMA 17 motors have one; a motor without it needs a magnet holder on the
   front shaft and a different mechanical layout.
2. Press the magnet onto the shaft centred. The [magnet tool](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files/Tools)
   in the firmware repository is a printed jig that centres it; a 3D-printed magnet spacer from
   [Stepper motor accessories](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files/Stepper%20motor%20accessories)
   fits between the shaft and the magnet when the shaft is too short.
3. Fix it with a drop of glue. A magnet that can turn on the shaft is the classic cause of a calibration that
   reports success and a motor that then runs badly: the magnet slipped between calibration and use.
4. Check the height after the board is mounted: with the spacer for your motor length, the gap is 1 mm. A magnet
   that touches the chip can destroy the microcontroller; a magnet 2 mm away or more gives a weak signal.

## Checking it

With the driver powered and the serial terminal open, `#Magnet` answers `Magnet Good` when the chip sees enough
field, `Magnet Bad` when it does not. The calibration routine runs the same test first. 

!!! warning "What the magnet test checks"
    Only that a magnet is close enough to the encoder. It passes with a magnet that is not glued, sits off-centre or
    can slip on the shaft, and fails only when there is no magnet or it is too far away. The 1 mm gap, the centring
    and the glue are yours to check.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/mounting/ -->

# Mounting on the motor

The board has the NEMA 17 hole pattern (31 mm), so it mounts on the back of the motor with the motor's own four
rear screws, with a spacer between the motor and the board that sets the magnet height.

1. Remove the four rear screws of the motor. They hold the motor's end cap; it does not come apart when you remove
   them one at a time and put the spacer and the board on at once.
2. Put the spacer on the motor. The firmware repository has printable spacers for common motor lengths in
   [Stepper motor accessories](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/STEPFOC-stepper-controller/tree/main/STEP%20files/Stepper%20motor%20accessories)
   (NEMA 17, a 21.5 mm NEMA 17 version, NEMA 23); for another motor, make a spacer that puts the board 1 mm above
   the magnet.
3. Put the board on the spacer, encoder chip towards the magnet, and fit longer screws of the same thread (M3 on a
   NEMA 17). Tighten them evenly; the board must be parallel to the magnet.
4. Check the gap: about 1 mm, the magnet not touching the chip.

A NEMA 14 or NEMA 23 motor needs an adapter plate between the motor and the board; the NEMA 23 spacer is in the
same folder.

!!! warning "The board is bare"
    Nothing on the back of the board may touch the motor's housing. Make sure the spacer keeps the board clear of
    the end cap, and keep metal swarf and screws away from the board while you work.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/wiring/ -->

# Wiring the stepper

A bipolar stepper has two coils and four wires. One coil goes to the terminals **A+ and A−**, the other to **B+
and B−**. Which coil is A and which is B does not matter, and neither does the polarity of each coil: firmware 105
and newer finds the wiring during calibration and compensates it.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Motor terminals and connectors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/STEPFOC_CONN.webp){ width="900" }
  <figcaption>Figure 7: The motor terminals A+, A−, B+, B− and the other connectors.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Finding the two coils

On most stepper motors the colours give the pairs away: **black and green** are one coil, **red and blue** the
other. The Stepperonline motors of [Tested motors](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/03-technical-data/tested-motors/) are wired that way:
black to A+, green to A−, red to B+, blue to B−.

| Coil | Usual wire colours | Terminals |
|---|---|---|
| A | black, green | A+, A− |
| B | red, blue | B+, B− |

Not every maker follows it, so check with a multimeter on the resistance range: the two wires of one coil show the
coil's resistance, a few ohms; two wires of different coils show no connection. Most datasheets also name the
pairs (A/C and B/D, or the colours).

## Soldering

1. Cut the leads to a comfortable length: long enough to reach the pads with the board mounted, short enough not to
   get into the motor's shaft. If your firmware is older than 105 (see [Releases and versions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/07-firmware/releases/)),
   leave them long enough to swap one pair later.
2. Tin the leads and solder them to the pads: one coil to A+ and A−, the other to B+ and B−.
3. Make sure no strand bridges two pads and that nothing touches the motor housing.

!!! warning
    Never connect or disconnect the motor while the driver is powered.

## Phase order and direction

Calibration spins the motor in open loop and watches the encoder. With firmware 105 and newer, a reversed coil is
detected and compensated in software (the firmware applies a reflection of the current frame, which is what a
physical swap would do), so the motor calibrates identically with any wiring, and positive commands turn the motor
counter-clockwise seen from the magnet side. With firmware 103, a reversed coil fails the open-loop step with
`Open loop: Failed / Switch motor phases and try again!`; swap A+ and A− and calibrate again.

If you want the other direction to be positive, swap the two wires of one coil and calibrate again, or keep the
wiring and use negative setpoints.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/power-and-can/ -->

# Power and the CAN daisy chain

Each driver has two power connectors (JST XH) and two CAN connectors (JST ZH). The second connector of each pair
feeds the next driver, so a chain of drivers hangs on one supply cable and one CAN cable.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![A daisy chain of drivers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/Daisy_chain-Photoroom.webp){ width="700" }
  <figcaption>Figure 8: Power and CAN pass from driver to driver. The first and the last node on the bus have their termination switch on.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Power

- 12 to 29 V DC, 24 V recommended. **DC+ to the positive supply, DC− to the negative**; reversed polarity destroys
  the driver.
- The power connectors are rated for 4 A. A chain of drivers shares that: with motors at 1.5 A each, plan for at
  most two or three drivers per chain that draw their full current at the same time, and feed a longer chain from
  both ends or from several supplies.
- A motor that decelerates pushes energy back into the supply. A lab supply or a battery absorbs it; a supply that
  cannot (some switch-mode supplies) sees its voltage rise, and the driver raises a Vbus error above 29.5 V.

## The cable orientation

!!! danger
    The daisy-chain cables are keyed by their orientation, not by the connector: the same 2-pin cable fits both
    ways, and the wrong way puts DC+ on DC−. Every cable must run as in the picture below, the same way at both
    ends. A wrong cable destroys the driver at the moment it is powered.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Cable orientation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/Orientation.webp){ width="600" }
  <figcaption>Figure 9: The orientation of the daisy-chain cables. The picture shows a generic 4-pin cable; the rule is the same for the 2-pin CAN and power cables.</figcaption>
</figure>

The cables from the shop are made this way: [CAN cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-can-cable),
[power cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-power-cable), and all of them under
[connectors and cables](https://source-robotics.com/pages/connectors-and-cables).

## CAN

- CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers. Up to 14 drivers on one bus, each with its own node ID, 0 to 13 (0 by default;
  set it with `#CANID` or Send_CAN_ID and save). The firmware accepts 14 and 15 too, but the
  [bootloader](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/07-firmware/the-bootloader/) reserves them: a driver on one of those IDs cannot be updated
  over CAN.
- Twisted-pair wire; keep the bus short at 1 Mbit/s (a few metres at most).
- **Termination:** the first and the last node on the bus need a 120 Ω resistor between CAN H and CAN L. The
  switch next to the CAN connectors turns the driver's resistor on (**ON**). Drivers in the middle stay off. A bus
  with the right termination measures about 60 Ω between CAN H and CAN L with everything unpowered.
- A PC joins the bus with the [CANvas adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter),
  which has its own termination.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The CAN termination switch](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/STEPFOC_CAN.webp){ width="520" }
  <figcaption>Figure 10: The termination switch, ON for the first and the last node.</figcaption>
</figure>


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/04-mounting/thermistor/ -->

# Thermistor

A 100 kΩ NTC thermistor on the motor lets the driver stop before the motor overheats. It is optional, and off by
default; use it on any motor that runs near its rated current for long.

!!! warning "Without it, nothing protects the motor from overheating"
    The driver limits the current, not the temperature. A motor that runs continuously, holds a load for long, or
    is set up badly (a current limit above its rating, loops that oscillate, a wrong resistance or inductance) can
    overheat and burn its windings without any warning. With the thermistor fitted and enabled, the driver stops
    first. The starter kit includes one.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![The thermistor connector](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/STEPFOC_THERMISTOR-Photoroom.webp){ width="520" }
  <figcaption>Figure 11: The thermistor on its 2-pin connector.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Fitting it

A stepper is sealed: the windings cannot be reached. Place the thermistor on the motor housing, as close to the
windings as possible: either glued to the side of the housing, or in one of the four screw holes of the motor's
bottom with the screw removed, which puts it deep in the stack. Thermal cement holds it and conducts the heat.

<figure markdown="span">
  ![Thermal cement](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/Thermal_cement.webp){ width="220" }
  <figcaption>Thermal cement: it sets hard and conducts heat. Thermal paste stays soft and lets the bead move, ordinary glue insulates it. <a href="https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_c3dBOwTD" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Where to buy it</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

The housing lags behind the windings by some seconds, and reads lower. Set the limit with that in mind: the
default of 75 °C at the housing corresponds to a hotter winding.

## Enabling it

```
#Term 1
#Tlim 75
#Save
```

`#Temp` then prints the temperature; with the thermistor disabled it prints `Temp Off`. Above the limit the driver
raises a temperature error and stops; it clears with `#Clear` once the motor has cooled.

Over CAN, Send_Respond_Temperature returns the temperature, and the temperature error is one of the bits of
Send_Respond_State_of_Errors.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/ -->

# First setup

From a mounted and wired driver to a calibrated, tuned motor. Motor GUI in the browser is the usual tool for it;
every step also gives the terminal command, for a terminal or for the console in Motor GUI.

1. [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/motor-gui/): the browser, the serial adapter, opening the port, what is on the screen.
2. [The serial terminal](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/terminal/): the alternative — PuTTY, the PlatformIO monitor or the Arduino monitor,
   and the `#` commands.
3. [Motor parameters and calibration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/calibration/): the factory defaults, the motor's resistance, inductance and pole pairs,
   then the calibration run.
4. [Current limit and loop tuning](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/tuning/): the current limit for the motor, and the loop gains if the
   defaults do not suit it.
5. [Saving the configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/saving/): nothing survives a power cycle until it is saved.

A driver that has been through these pages is ready for [Operation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/06-operation/). The
[Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/quick-start/) is the same path on one page.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/05-setup/motor-gui/ -->

# Motor GUI

[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) is the usual way to set up, test and tune a driver: a tool in the browser that
connects to one driver over the serial adapter or to a bus of drivers over the CANvas adapter, shows the state,
moves the motor, runs the calibration, tunes the loops with live plots, records telemetry and updates the
firmware. Nothing is installed. Everything it does, the driver also does from a terminal or from Python — the
GUI reads and writes the same settings — so every procedure in this manual shows the GUI first and the terminal
command beside it.

## The browser

Motor GUI reaches the hardware through the browser's serial port access (Web Serial), which Chromium-based
browsers have: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera. Firefox and Safari cannot open serial ports.

## Two ways to connect

| | Adapter | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| **One driver over serial** | the 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter on the driver's UART connector, 256000 baud | the first setup and calibration (calibration runs over UART only), tuning on the bench |
| **A bus over CAN** | the CANvas adapter; it appears as a serial port and speaks slcan | every driver on the bus by its node ID: testing a machine, updating firmware on all joints |

## Opening the port

1. Plug in the adapter and the motor supply. The adapter alone powers the driver's logic, enough to open the
   port and read the settings, but the driver reports a Vbus error and will not calibrate or move until the
   supply is on.
2. Open [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/), choose the connection kind, and **Connect**. The browser asks
   which port; pick the adapter's.
3. The driver's identity appears: hardware version, firmware version, serial number, batch date, whether it is
   calibrated and activated, and the active errors — what `#Info` prints in a terminal.

If the port is not offered, the browser is not Chromium-based, or another program holds the port (a terminal left
open, PlatformIO's monitor). If the port opens and nothing appears: the driver is unpowered, or TX and RX are
crossed on an adapter that is not the Source Robotics one.

## What is on the screen

- **State**: the identity above, the control mode the driver is in, the errors, and **Clear errors**.
- **Jog**: *Jog position*, *Jog velocity* and *Jog current* move the motor in the matching control mode; *Send
  setpoint* sends a value in the current mode. *Live stream while dragging* follows a slider as you move it.
- **Plots** of position, speed and current, panning and zooming, with the value under the pointer.
- **Settings**: the motor parameters (pole pairs, resistance, inductance), the limits (current, velocity,
  voltage), the loop gains with *Apply gains* and *Apply preset*, the CAN node ID, the watchdog, the thermistor.
  The GUI marks *Unsaved changes* until you **Save** to the driver's EEPROM; *Default* restores the factory values.
- **Calibration**: starts `#Cal` and shows the driver's log step by step; afterwards the phase order and
  direction, Kt, KV and the flux linkage it found.
- **Telemetry**: the stream from the driver, and recordings of it for a test or a bug report.
- **Firmware update**: the releases from GitHub, flashed through the bootloader; *Scan bootloaders* on a bus.
- **Gripper**: the gripper controls, for a driver in gripper mode.
- **Console**: type any `#` command by hand; the answer appears below it.
- **Wiring diagrams** and **Keyboard shortcuts** under help.

## Screen guide

<figure class="gui-shot" markdown="1">
<div class="gui-shot__image" markdown="1">

<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:3%;top:20%" aria-hidden="true">1</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:15%;top:20%" aria-hidden="true">2</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:23%;top:20%" aria-hidden="true">3</span>

</div>
<figcaption markdown="1">**1. Transport:** choose UART for the serial adapter. **2. Baud:** 256000 for a stock driver. **3. Connect:** choose the adapter in the browser's port picker.</figcaption>
</figure>

<figure class="gui-shot" markdown="1">
<div class="gui-shot__image" markdown="1">

![Motor GUI simulated motor: device state, controls and live telemetry](https://docs.source-robotics.com/STEPFOC-docs/108/assets/motor-gui/motor-demo.jpg){ width="1000" }

<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:1%;top:9%" aria-hidden="true">1</span>

</div>
